blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A booking service on Java 21 reads each uploaded guest list with `String text = new String(body);`. Its servers run with a Latin-1 locale and no `-Dfile.encoding` option. A hotel uploads a list saved as ISO-8859-1 containing the line `Peña;Zürich`. What does the service get for the `ñ` and the `ü`?

options.text: Each becomes U+FFFD, since the default charset is UTF-8 and the file's Latin-1 bytes for them aren't valid UTF-8
options.says: since Java 18 the default charset is UTF-8 whatever the locale, and new String(bytes) replaces what it can't decode

options.text: Each becomes two characters, such as `Ã±`, since the default charset is UTF-8 and reads their bytes one at a time
options.says: that is UTF-8 bytes read as Latin-1; here Latin-1 bytes are read as UTF-8, and the bytes it can't decode become U+FFFD

options.text: Each comes through as the hotel wrote it, since the default charset comes from the locale and matches the file's
options.says: the locale set the default charset only up to Java 17; since Java 18 the default is UTF-8

options.text: Each becomes `?`, since the default charset comes from the locale and its Latin-1 has no room for letters outside ASCII
options.says: the default is UTF-8 since Java 18, and new String(bytes) replaces what it can't decode with U+FFFD; `?` is what encoding puts for an unencodable character

origin.section: Bytes Become Text Only Through a Charset, and new String(bytes) Picks One for You

questions.stem: An audit service keeps its last 200,000 request descriptions in memory, each about 500 ASCII characters, and runs with default JVM settings. A release puts a check mark `✓` (U+2713) at the start of every description. How does the heap those descriptions hold change?

options.text: It grows by about 3 bytes per description, since U+2713 takes three bytes in UTF-8 and the other characters keep one each
options.says: three bytes is the check mark's UTF-8 size; the heap doesn't store strings as UTF-8

options.text: It grows by about 2 bytes per description, since U+2713 takes two bytes in UTF-16 and the other characters keep one each
options.says: the encoding is chosen for the whole string: one character above U+00FF moves every character to two bytes

options.text: It roughly doubles, since U+2713 doesn't fit in one byte and so every character of the string moves to two bytes
options.says: compact strings keep a string in Latin-1 only while all its characters fit; otherwise the whole string is UTF-16

options.text: It hardly changes, since U+2713 fits in one UTF-16 char and every character was already stored in two bytes
options.says: since Java 9 a string whose characters all fit in Latin-1 takes one byte per character

origin.section: A String Keeps Latin-1 Text at One Byte per Character, and One Character Beyond Latin-1 Doubles It

questions.stem: A session store keeps 3 million sessions in memory. Each session's `locale` is parsed from a request header and takes one of about 40 values. To save heap, a developer changes the code that fills it to `String locale = parseLocale(header); locale.intern(); session.setLocale(locale);`. What happens to the heap the locales take?

options.text: It drops to about 40 strings, since intern() replaces the variable's copy with the pooled one
options.says: intern() returns the pooled string; it can't change the string or the variable it is called on, and the session stores that variable

options.text: It stays about the same, since text read at run time is kept out of the pool, which holds the code's literals
options.says: intern() adds a string to the pool when no equal one is there, so later calls with that text find it

options.text: It drops to about 40 strings, since the collector merges copies equal to a pooled one into it
options.says: the pool shares a string only with code that stores what intern() returns

options.text: It stays about the same, since intern() hands back the pooled copy but each session gets the parser's copy
options.says: the returned reference is dropped, so each session keeps its own copy and nothing is shared

origin.section: Equal Strings Built at Run Time Are Separate Objects; intern() Shares One Only with Code That Keeps Its Result

questions.stem: A chat server decodes each incoming message into one reusable `char[] buf` and keeps `String user = new String(buf, 0, n);` in a map of connected users. The next message from another client then overwrites `buf`. What does the map hold for the first user afterwards?

options.text: The next message's characters, since the String reads its characters from buf each time it is used
options.says: the constructor copies the characters; the String holds no reference to buf

options.text: The first message's characters, since the String took its own copy of them when it was constructed
options.says: every String constructor that takes an array copies it, so later changes to the array don't reach the String

options.text: The next message's characters, since the String and buf share one array until one of the two is changed
options.says: no String shares an array with code outside the class; the copy happens in the constructor

options.text: The first message's characters, since a write to buf goes to a fresh array once a String refers to the old one
options.says: nothing locks the array; the String is unaffected because it holds a copy

origin.section: A String Copies What It Is Built From, So Nothing Changes It Afterwards

concepts: A String built from an array copies it, and toCharArray returns a copy, so later changes to the array never reach the String.
Since Java 18 the default charset is UTF-8 whatever the operating system's locale.
